column1: # Plates first checked for the household binder (images/plants.json there), reused with captions reworded for the kit.

column4: caption
A flowering stand at a field edge: tall, with a mass of white flower umbrellas. This is how you usually meet it.
THE FEATURE THAT MATTERS: the smooth, hairless green stem with purple-to-maroon blotches.
The leaf: finely divided, fern-like and glossy. Smell proves nothing; identify by stem, leaf and habitat.
The flower head: small white flowers in a loose, domed umbrella.
Botanical line drawing of the whole plant: branching habit, compound toothed leaves, and the fruit enlarged.
The flower head: dense, flat and lacy, often with a single dark purple floret in the centre.
Underneath the flower head: a ring of long, forked green bracts, and the hairy stem.
The seed head curling inward into a "bird's nest" as it dries.
Botanical line drawing: the coarsely toothed compound leaves and the flat flower head. The flowers are YELLOW, not white.
The flat, ribbed seeds (scale bar shown).
THREE LEAFLETS on one stalk, the middle leaflet on a longer stalk than the two side ones. Leaf edges vary on the same plant.
The same three-leaflet pattern with a glossier surface, climbing.
Botanical line drawing: the three-leaflet leaves and the clusters of dull WHITE berries.
THE DANGEROUS STAGE: grass-like folded leaves from a bulb, no flower yet. No onion smell means not onion.
The flower spike: creamy-white six-parted flowers with a green gland at the base of each petal.
Botanical line drawing: the bulb, the grass-like leaves and the flower spike together.
Pink-to-white flower clusters on slender stalks above narrow, flat leaves.
Botanical line drawing: the bulb with its fibrous coat, the slender leaves and the flower cluster.
The flowers: purple swept-back petals around a pointed yellow cone.
The berries, ripening from green through orange to glossy red, hanging in small clusters. This is what a small child reaches for.
Buds and young flowers on the vine, with the leaf shape visible.
A whole plant: the flat rosette of deeply toothed leaves, with flower stalks and seed heads.
Flowers in a lawn: one solid yellow head per hollow, leafless stalk.
The seed head opening: the white "clock".
A broad oval leaf with strong parallel veins, and the narrow green flower spike.
The whole rosette flat against the ground, with spikes rising from the centre.
Botanical line drawing: the parallel-veined leaf, the spike and the fibrous roots.
The whole plant: upright and branching, with diamond-to-triangular leaves and dense greenish flower spikes.
Botanical line drawing: the leaf shape and the flower cluster, with the seed enlarged.
Botanical line drawing: the sprawling stems, thick paddle-shaped succulent leaves and small flowers. No public-domain photograph was found; learn it in person.
The stem covered in stinging hairs, with paired leaves.
Leaves in opposite pairs: coarsely toothed, pointed tips.
Drooping greenish flower strings hanging from the leaf joints.
The brown seed-head spike, the feature everyone recognises. Harvest shoots only from stands identified by these spikes.
Green flowering spikes among the long flat leaves, standing in shallow water.
A dense stand at the water's edge: the habitat, and the water to judge for contamination.
Leaves and the long cylindrical brush of small white flowers.
Fruit clusters on the branch, with the leaf shape clear (black and white).
Botanical line drawing of leaf, flower cluster and fruit.
A wild plum thicket along a field edge.
A flowering branch: five-petalled white flowers before or with the leaves (black and white).
Botanical line drawing of leaf, flower and fruit, with the plum whole and in section.
Leaves and a white five-petalled flower; leaflets white-woolly underneath, on a prickly cane.
Botanical line drawing of cane, leaves, flower and fruit.
The whole plant: stout stem, dense bristly green flower spike, oval pointed leaves.
Botanical line drawing: the leaf, the bristly seed head and flowers enlarged.
A bur oak leaf on its own bark: the deeply lobed leaf and the thick, ridged grey bark.
Leaves with an acorn: the big acorn in a deep, shaggy fringed cap.
Mature trunk bark close up: deep vertical furrows (black and white).
An ash leaf on ash bark: a compound leaf, and bark in a tight diamond pattern.
Trunk bark: interlacing diamond ridges (black and white).
An elm leaf on elm bark: the leaf base is LOPSIDED and the edge doubly toothed.
A hackberry leaf on hackberry bark, which is covered in corky warts and ridges.
The warty, knobbly bark close up.
The large compound leaf: many paired leaflets along one stalk.
Bark: dark, deeply furrowed into narrow ridges in a rough diamond pattern.
A cottonwood leaf on furrowed grey bark: a broad triangle with coarse rounded teeth.
Leaf detail: the flattened leaf stalk that makes the leaves rattle in a breeze.
The compound leaf: three to five leaflets on one stalk, often irregularly lobed.
Typical form: a low, spreading, multi-stemmed tree of fence lines.
